subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

periods.stage_label: Observe and sort — magnetic vs non-magnetic
periods.activity_description: Students collect classroom objects, record predictions about magnetic attraction, then test each object with a bar magnet and enter observations in a two-column results table. They sort objects into magnetic and non-magnetic groups and identify the pattern in materials that respond.

roles.role_description: Distributes magnets and object sets, poses the opening prediction question, and circulates to prompt accurate recording.
Predict, test each object systematically, record results, and sort objects into the two named categories.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Reshma's compass story from the chapter and poses the driving question: which everyday things does a magnet pull?
Groups predict for each object — attracted or not — and record predictions before touching the magnet to anything.
Groups test each object with the bar magnet, record actual results alongside predictions, and physically separate the objects into two piles.
Whole-class share-out: which materials attracted? Students name the categories magnetic and non-magnetic, and teacher introduces the terms iron, nickel, cobalt as examples of magnetic materials.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit anchors the chapter in hands-on prediction and testing — the same spirit as Activity 4.1 in the chapter. Watch for the common error that all metals are magnetic; several objects in the set (aluminium foil, copper coin) are metallic but non-magnetic, and surfacing this contrast early prevents the misconception from hardening. A useful checkpoint before moving on: every group should be able to state at least two magnetic and two non-magnetic materials by name.
materials: Assorted objects: iron nail, steel spoon, aluminium foil, copper coin, rubber eraser, wooden stick, plastic ruler, glass marble, paper clip

periods.stage_label: Observe and sort — magnetic vs non-magnetic
periods.activity_title: Sorting by evidence — refining the categories
periods.activity_description: Students revisit their results table from the previous unit, discuss anomalies (metallic but non-magnetic items), and propose a refined rule for what makes a material magnetic. They then classify a new set of five unlabelled material strips using only their magnet, recording justifications for each classification.

roles.role_description: Facilitates discussion of anomalies and probes students' emerging rule with targeted questions.
Each student writes a one-sentence rule explaining why some materials are magnetic, then tests the five new strips independently and justifies each classification in writing.

time_bands.activity: Small-group discussion of previous unit results: which predictions were wrong, and what do the magnetic materials have in common?
Each student writes a personal rule for magnetic materials on their worksheet, then shares with a partner to compare.
Students test five unlabelled material strips with the magnet and write a classification (magnetic or non-magnetic) with a one-sentence justification for each.
Class compares classifications; teacher consolidates the rule: iron, nickel, cobalt and some alloys are magnetic — the category is specific, not all metals.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the two categories; this unit deepens the reasoning by asking students to articulate a rule before testing. The most persistent misconception here is that 'heavy' or 'shiny' materials are magnetic — probe this directly if it appears in students' written rules. If groups finish the strip-testing quickly, ask them to predict whether a magnet would attract another magnet and save that question as a hook for the poles unit coming next.
materials: Five unlabelled strips (e.g. iron, aluminium, copper, plastic, stainless steel)

periods.stage_label: Investigate — where is the force strongest?
periods.activity_description: Students spread iron filings on a sheet of paper, lay a bar magnet beneath, and tap gently. They observe and sketch the pattern of filings, noting that the filings cluster most densely at the two ends. They repeat with a U-shaped magnet to confirm that poles occur at the ends regardless of shape.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates safe handling of iron filings and circulates to ensure students tap gently and observe before disturbing the pattern.
Lay the magnet, tap the paper, sketch the observed pattern, annotate where filings are densest, and repeat with the U-shaped magnet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit: students sorted materials by whether a magnet attracts them — now the question shifts to where along the magnet the pull is strongest.
Groups spread iron filings, place the bar magnet beneath the paper, tap gently, and sketch the filing pattern; they annotate which zones are densest.
Groups repeat with a U-shaped magnet and note whether the dense zones appear at the same relative positions.
Whole-class comparison of sketches; teacher introduces the term poles, names them North and South, and states that every magnet has exactly two poles regardless of shape.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves from classifying materials to investigating the spatial distribution of magnetic force — a meaningful step up in cognitive demand from the previous stage. A common error is assuming the middle of the magnet is also strongly magnetic; the iron filings make the weak middle zone visible, so highlight it explicitly. Ask groups to compare bar and U-shaped magnet sketches side by side: the structural similarity of poles-at-ends is the key insight to consolidate before the next unit.

periods.stage_label: Investigate — where is the force strongest?
periods.activity_title: Can you isolate a single pole?
periods.activity_description: Students cut a bar magnet-shaped paper strip labelled N–S, then consider what would happen if a real magnet were broken in half. They test this idea with the iron filings pattern on a broken or snapped ferrite strip (or reason through it if physical breaking is not possible), recording what they observe about the new ends and proposing an explanation.

roles.role_description: Poses the inquiry question and either provides pre-broken ferrite strips or guides a structured reasoning exercise if physical breaking is unsafe.
Test or reason about the broken magnet, record what happens to the poles, and propose a written explanation of why a single pole cannot be isolated.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question: if a magnet has two poles and we cut it in half, what do we get — one pole each, or something else?
Groups either test pre-broken ferrite strips with iron filings to reveal new poles, or reason through a diagram of successive breaks and predict what is found at each new end.
Groups write a short explanation: why does every fragment of a broken magnet still have both a North and a South pole?
Share-out and consolidation: teacher confirms the chapter's key statement — poles always exist in pairs; no isolated magnetic pole has ever been observed.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established that poles are the sites of strongest force; this unit challenges students to reason about what poles fundamentally are rather than just locate them. Students often expect that breaking a magnet gives one N-pole piece and one S-pole piece — surfacing and correcting this misconception is the central purpose of the unit. If pre-broken ferrite strips are not available, a carefully drawn diagram exercise achieves the same reasoning goal and satisfies the chapter's own treatment of this concept.
materials: Pre-broken ferrite magnet strips (or diagram worksheet if unavailable)

periods.stage_label: Explain — Earth's magnetism and directional alignment
periods.activity_description: Students suspend a bar magnet freely by a thread, let it settle, mark the resting line on paper beneath, disturb the magnet, and repeat. They record that the magnet always returns to the same north–south line, then compare by suspending an unmagnetised iron bar and observing that it rests in any direction.

roles.role_description: Sets up the suspension point and guides students to mark resting positions carefully across multiple trials.
Suspend the magnet, mark each resting line, disturb and repeat at least three times, then suspend the iron bar and record the contrast.

time_bands.activity: Teacher links to the previous stage: students now know where the force is concentrated — this unit asks why a freely suspended magnet always points the same way.
Groups suspend the bar magnet, let it settle, mark the line, disturb gently, and repeat; they record whether the resting direction is consistent across trials.
Groups replace the magnet with an unmagnetised iron bar and record which direction it settles in, noting any difference from the magnet's behaviour.
Class discussion: what force causes the consistent alignment? Teacher introduces Earth as a giant magnet and names the North-seeking and South-seeking poles.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the shift from investigating where the force is to explaining why a magnet behaves as it does in Earth's field — a genuine causal step up from Stage 2. Watch for students who assume any elongated object will align north–south; the iron bar control directly counters this. The contrast between the magnet's consistent settling and the iron bar's random settling is the pivot of the explanation, so give groups enough time to complete both observations before the class discussion.
materials: Unmagnetised iron bars or thick iron nails
Paper sheets for marking resting lines

periods.stage_label: Explain — Earth's magnetism and directional alignment
periods.activity_description: Students magnetise an iron sewing needle by stroking it repeatedly with one pole of a bar magnet, mount the needle through a cork floating in a water-filled dish, and observe which end points north. They then compare their floating compass with a commercial magnetic compass and record whether both indicate the same direction.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the stroking technique for magnetisation and ensures all groups use unidirectional strokes before independent work.
Magnetise the needle using repeated unidirectional strokes, mount it on the cork, float it, and record the needle's resting direction and comparison with the commercial compass.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates correct magnetisation by stroking: always in one direction, lifting the magnet between strokes — students watch before attempting.
Groups stroke the needle at least twenty times, mount it through a cork, float the assembly in water, and observe and record which end points north after the needle settles.
Groups place a commercial compass beside the floating compass and record whether both needles point in the same direction.
Class consolidation: teacher connects to the matsya-yantra sidebar and explains how the compass structure — freely rotating magnetised needle — embodies Earth's directional property.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the principle of north–south alignment; this unit has students construct the very instrument that makes that principle practical, reinforcing the explanation through making. The most common error is stroking back and forth, which partially demagnetises the needle — insist on unidirectional strokes before groups begin independently. Comparing the homemade and commercial compass readings gives students direct evidence that the same magnetic principle underlies both devices.
materials: Shallow dishes or bowls with water
Commercial magnetic compasses (one per group or for demonstration)

periods.stage_label: Investigate interactions — attraction and repulsion between poles
periods.activity_title: Like poles push, unlike poles pull
periods.activity_description: Students place a bar magnet on pencils so it can roll freely, then systematically bring the four pole combinations of a second magnet toward the resting magnet and observe whether it moves toward or away. They record results in a table of pole pairs and state the attraction–repulsion rule in their own words.

roles.role_description: Sets up the rolling magnet demonstration and ensures pole labels are clearly marked on all magnets before groups begin.
Test all four pole-pair combinations, record the direction of movement or the absence of movement, and write a summary rule.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to earlier stages: students know poles are the sites of strongest force — now they investigate what happens when two poles meet.
Groups test N–N, S–S, N–S, and S–N combinations with the rolling magnet and record observed movement (toward / away / no movement) for each.
Groups replace the approaching magnet with an iron bar and repeat the test, recording whether the iron bar also causes the rolling magnet to move away.
Pairs share their written rule; class agrees on the formulation: like poles repel, unlike poles attract — and repulsion is the test that distinguishes a magnet from plain iron.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 4, which raises cognitive demand to the level of interaction and causal reasoning between two objects. Students often predict symmetry without distinguishing attraction from repulsion by direction of movement — the rolling magnet setup makes the difference unmistakable. The iron-bar comparison at the end of the activity is essential: it is the chapter's own definitive test for identifying a true magnet, and should be treated as a conclusion, not an afterthought.
materials: Two bar magnets per group (poles clearly labelled N and S)
Three or four round pencils per group for the rolling surface
Iron bar or large iron nail

periods.stage_label: Investigate interactions — attraction and repulsion between poles
periods.activity_title: Compass needle as a pole detector
periods.activity_description: Students use a magnetic compass as a live indicator of pole interactions: they bring the North pole of a bar magnet toward the compass needle's North end and record what the needle does, then bring the South pole and record again. They then design a two-step test using only the compass to determine which end of an unmarked bar is the North pole.

roles.role_description: Introduces the compass as a detection tool and poses the design challenge for the unmarked-bar test.
Carry out the two pole-approach observations, record the needle's response, and write out the two-step procedure for identifying the North pole of an unmarked bar.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the link question: the previous unit used movement of a rolling magnet to detect repulsion — can a compass needle serve the same function?
Students bring the bar magnet's North pole near the compass needle's North end; record the response; repeat with the South pole; record again.
Each student writes a two-step procedure for using only a compass to identify the North pole of an unmarked bar magnet, drawing on the repulsion observation.
Students exchange procedures with a neighbour for peer review, then a few procedures are shared and refined with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the rule; this unit asks students to apply that rule instrumentally — using the compass as a detector and designing their own test procedure. A common confusion is expecting the compass needle to always point toward any magnet regardless of which poles face each other; the repulsion observation corrects this. The procedure-writing task is the first time in this chapter that students author a test rather than follow one, which is an appropriate escalation of inquiry at this stage.
materials: Magnetic compasses (one per student or pair)
Worksheet for recording responses and writing procedures

periods.stage_label: Investigate interactions — attraction and repulsion between poles
periods.activity_title: Does a barrier stop the magnetic effect?
periods.activity_description: Students interpose sheets of wood, cardboard, plastic, and glass one at a time between a bar magnet and a compass, recording the needle's deflection angle each time and comparing it to the deflection without any barrier. They use their results to conclude whether non-magnetic materials block or transmit the magnetic effect.

roles.role_description: Sets a fixed magnet-to-compass distance for all groups so results are comparable, and guides students to read the compass scale consistently.
Insert each barrier material in turn, read and record the compass needle deflection, and compare deflections to draw a conclusion about transmission of magnetic effect.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous two units and poses the new question: the interaction between poles has been established — can a non-magnetic material placed between them stop it?
Groups test each barrier material — wood, cardboard, plastic, glass — recording the compass needle deflection angle with each material interposed.
Groups compare all recorded deflections with the no-barrier baseline and write a conclusion sentence about whether non-magnetic materials block the magnetic effect.
Class shares conclusions; teacher generalises: magnetic effects act through non-magnetic materials, which is why magnets can be used to guide steel balls through a cardboard maze.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit closes Stage 4 by extending the concept of magnetic interaction to include the transmission of force through intervening materials — a subtler property not addressed in the first two stages. Students commonly predict that any solid barrier will weaken the effect, so the stable needle deflection across all non-magnetic barriers is genuinely surprising and worth pausing on. The cardboard maze application from the Fun with Magnets section makes a natural closing link and previews the next stage.
materials: Sheets of wood, cardboard, plastic, and glass (sized to fit between magnet and compass)

periods.stage_label: Apply and investigate — using magnet properties in unfamiliar contexts
periods.activity_title: Magnetic maze and garland — properties in play
periods.activity_description: Students guide a steel ball through a cardboard maze using a magnet held beneath, and construct a hanging chain of paper clips from a single magnet. They record which magnet property each application exploits and explain in writing why the application works, referencing specific properties established in earlier stages.

roles.role_description: Provides the maze and paper-clip materials and challenges each group to name the specific property at work before they begin.
Run both applications, record which property each exploits, and write a one-paragraph explanation connecting observation to the properties of poles, magnetic materials, and force transmission.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the two playful challenges from the Fun with Magnets section and asks groups to predict which magnet properties will be needed.
Groups guide the steel ball through the maze using the under-magnet technique and record which property allows the magnet to act through the cardboard base.
Groups hang a chain of paper clips from one pole of a magnet, observe how many clips the chain holds, and record what this reveals about the distribution of magnetic force.
Groups write connecting explanations and share two: the class identifies which chapter properties — attraction, poles, force through non-magnetic materials — each application draws on.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 5, where the cognitive demand shifts from investigating properties within controlled setups to applying those properties to explain novel situations. Students may name attraction as the only relevant property — probe them to also name force transmission through non-magnetic materials (maze) and pole-strength concentration (garland chain). The written explanation is the key product here: it is the first time students must integrate multiple properties into a single account.
materials: Steel balls or small ball bearings
Cardboard sheets to form maze walls
Worksheets for recording and writing explanations

periods.stage_label: Apply and investigate — using magnet properties in unfamiliar contexts
periods.activity_title: Magnet in water — and keeping magnets safe
periods.activity_description: Students use a magnet to retrieve a steel paper clip submerged in water without touching the water, record observations about the force acting through water, and then examine care-and-storage instructions for magnets, applying the attraction–repulsion rule to explain why unlike-poles-adjacent storage is recommended.

roles.role_description: Sets up the water retrieval challenge and provides storage instruction text from the chapter for groups to analyse.
Retrieve the clip, record observations, then read the storage instructions and write a property-based explanation for each care rule.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the water-retrieval challenge and asks students to predict whether water, like the non-magnetic solids tested earlier, will transmit the magnetic effect.
Groups retrieve the submerged clip with the magnet, record their observation, and write a one-sentence explanation linking the result to the barrier-transmission findings from the previous stage.
Groups read the storage instructions (unlike poles adjacent, wooden separator, keeper bars, avoid heat/dropping) and write a property-based reason for each rule.
Groups share their explanations for the storage rules; class consolidates: storage recommendations are logical consequences of the properties studied throughout the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit continues Stage 5 by presenting two further application contexts — water as a medium and practical care — that require students to extend what they already know rather than learn new facts. The water challenge is a natural extension of the non-magnetic-barrier finding from the previous stage, and students who grasped that result should predict the outcome correctly. The storage analysis is more demanding because it asks students to reason backward from a rule to its property-based justification, which is the kind of causal reasoning the final stage targets.
materials: Bowls or shallow trays with water
Printed or written excerpt of storage instructions from the chapter

periods.stage_label: Apply and investigate — using magnet properties in unfamiliar contexts
periods.activity_title: Unknown object, unknown magnet — a full investigation
periods.activity_description: Each group receives an unmarked object (either a magnet or an iron bar) and must design and carry out a multi-step test sequence using only available classroom materials to determine whether the object is a magnet, a magnetic material, or a non-magnetic material, and if it is a magnet, to identify its North pole.

roles.role_description: Distributes unmarked objects and prompts groups to plan their test sequence in writing before touching any materials.
Write a planned test sequence, carry out the tests, record each result, and state a final evidence-based conclusion about the nature and pole identity of the object.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes unmarked objects and asks each group to write a multi-step test plan before beginning — which properties will they test, in what order, and what each result will mean.

Groups carry out their planned tests in sequence, recording the result of each step and annotating whether each result is consistent with the object being a magnet, magnetic material, or non-magnetic material.
Groups formulate a final written conclusion: what is the object, and — if it is a magnet — which end is North, and what evidence supports each claim.
Two or three groups share their test sequences and conclusions; the class evaluates whether the evidence is sufficient and whether any test could be improved.

periods.teacher_notes: This final unit asks students to orchestrate all the properties they have investigated across the chapter — attraction, pole strength, directional alignment, repulsion as a magnet test — into a coherent self-designed investigation of an unknown object. The most telling difference between strong and weak responses will be whether students include repulsion as a step: attraction alone cannot distinguish a magnet from magnetic iron, but repulsion from a known pole can. The closing share-out also invites students to critique one another's test designs, which is the highest-demand move of the chapter.
materials: Unmarked objects: a mix of bar magnets, iron bars, and non-magnetic rods (one per group, identity unknown to students)

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and sort — magnetic vs non-magnetic
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students test and classify everyday objects as magnetic or non-magnetic using a bar magnet, record results in a table, and articulate a rule identifying which materials respond to a magnet.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can sort a given set of objects into magnetic and non-magnetic categories using a magnet, and state a rule identifying iron, nickel, cobalt, and some alloys as the magnetic materials, with written justification for each classification.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Investigate — where is the force strongest?
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use iron filings to reveal that magnetic force concentrates at a magnet's poles, sketch the filing pattern for bar and U-shaped magnets, and reason about why breaking a magnet cannot produce a single isolated pole.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can sketch the iron-filings pattern showing pole concentration, name the poles North and South, and explain with evidence why every fragment of a broken magnet retains both poles.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain — Earth's magnetism and directional alignment
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students suspend a bar magnet and an iron bar to compare their resting directions, explain the consistent north–south alignment using Earth's magnetic nature, and construct a floating compass that confirms the directional property.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why a freely suspended magnet always aligns north–south by connecting it to Earth acting as a giant magnet, and can distinguish a magnet from an unmagnetised bar using the directional test.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Investigate interactions — attraction and repulsion between poles
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students test all four pole-pair combinations with a rolling magnet and a compass needle, establish the like-repels unlike-attracts rule, use repulsion to design a test for an unmarked bar, and investigate whether non-magnetic barriers block the magnetic effect.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can state and apply the attraction–repulsion rule for pole pairs, use repulsion as the definitive test for identifying a magnet, and conclude from evidence that non-magnetic materials do not block magnetic effects.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply and investigate — using magnet properties in unfamiliar contexts
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students apply all established magnet properties to explain playful applications, retrieve a clip from water, reason about magnet storage rules, and design and carry out a self-planned multi-step investigation to identify an unknown object and determine its pole orientation.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can design and execute a multi-step investigation to determine whether an unknown object is a magnet, a magnetic material, or a non-magnetic material — including pole identification — by selecting and sequencing relevant property tests and defending each conclusion with evidence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and sort — magnetic vs non-magnetic
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sort a given set of objects into magnetic and non-magnetic categories using a bar magnet, and state a rule identifying iron, nickel, cobalt, and some alloys as the magnetic materials, with written justification for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: A student tests five objects with a bar magnet: an aluminium foil strip, an iron nail, a copper coin, a nickel coin, and a plastic ruler. Which pair of objects will both be attracted to the magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: Aluminium foil strip and copper coin

options.label: B
options.text: Copper coin and nickel coin

options.label: C
options.text: Iron nail and aluminium foil strip

options.label: D
options.text: Iron nail and nickel coin

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing aluminium and copper reveals the misconception that all metals are magnetic, failing to distinguish between the specific metals (iron, nickel, cobalt) that respond to a magnet.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing iron and aluminium shows partial knowledge — iron is correctly identified as magnetic but aluminium is incorrectly included because it is a shiny, metallic-looking material.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing copper and nickel shows confusion between the two non-ferrous metals and the magnetic metal nickel; the student may be recalling names without connecting them to magnetic behaviour.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with recall of specific metals can be encouraged to reason from the rule they wrote in the activity: does the material contain iron, nickel, or cobalt? Students with strong visual memory may have marked their results table with colour codes that they can mentally reference.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and sort — magnetic vs non-magnetic
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sort a given set of objects into magnetic and non-magnetic categories using a bar magnet, and state a rule identifying iron, nickel, cobalt, and some alloys as the magnetic materials, with written justification for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: Which of the following correctly completes the rule: 'Materials attracted to a magnet are called magnetic materials. These are always ___'?

options.label: A
options.text: Heavy materials

options.label: B
options.text: Iron, nickel, cobalt, or some of their alloys

options.label: C
options.text: Metals

options.label: D
options.text: Shiny or smooth materials

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'metals' reflects the most common misconception in this chapter — that all metals respond to magnets — without distinguishing the specific group of magnetic materials.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'heavy materials' reflects a physical-appearance heuristic; the student has not connected magnetic behaviour to material composition but to an observable physical property.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'shiny or smooth materials' similarly reflects a surface-appearance heuristic rather than understanding based on material type — a misconception that hands-on testing of dull iron versus shiny copper should have addressed.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who learned the rule by testing objects can approach this question by mentally replaying which objects attracted the magnet; verbalising the rule before reading the options is a useful strategy for students who process better orally.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate — where is the force strongest?
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sketch the iron-filings pattern showing pole concentration, name the poles North and South, and explain with evidence why every fragment of a broken magnet retains both poles.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: When iron filings are spread on a paper placed over a bar magnet, they cluster most densely at the two ends and very sparsely in the middle. What does this pattern tell us about the magnetic force along the bar magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: The magnetic force is equal at all points along the magnet.

options.label: B
options.text: The magnetic force is strongest at the centre of the magnet.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnetic force is strongest at the two ends, called poles, and weakest in the middle.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnetic force only exists at whichever end faces north.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing uniform force shows the student did not connect the uneven distribution of iron filings to the uneven distribution of magnetic force — they may have not attended to the density gradient in the activity.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing the centre reflects an intuitive but incorrect assumption that the strongest part of any object is its middle, unconnected to observation of the filings pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing the north-pointing end only conflates the directional property (which end points north) from Stage 3 with the force-distribution property being tested here — a cross-stage confusion.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who sketched the filing pattern during the activity can mentally replay the sketch; encouraging them to draw a quick bar with filings distribution before answering benefits kinaesthetic learners.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate — where is the force strongest?
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sketch the iron-filings pattern showing pole concentration, name the poles North and South, and explain with evidence why every fragment of a broken magnet retains both poles.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: A student breaks a bar magnet into three pieces and brings a compass near each piece. What will the compass show for every piece, no matter how small?

options.label: A
options.text: Each piece will have only one pole — the middle piece will have no pole at all.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the two end pieces retain poles; the middle piece becomes non-magnetic.

options.label: C
options.text: Each piece will have both a North pole and a South pole.

options.label: D
options.text: The pieces will retain their original poles only if they are larger than half the original magnet.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing one pole per piece reflects the intuitive but incorrect prediction that breaking the magnet simply divides the poles — exactly the misconception the inquiry activity on breaking was designed to address.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing end-pieces only shows a partial correction — the student accepts that the original ends keep poles but has not generalised that every fragment, including the middle, becomes a complete small magnet.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing size as a threshold introduces an invented rule with no grounding in the chapter, suggesting the student is guessing rather than applying the poles-always-in-pairs principle.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who find abstract reasoning difficult, suggesting they mentally walk through the diagram of successive breaks from the activity — each new cut face becomes a new pole — makes the principle concrete and reachable.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate — where is the force strongest?
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sketch the iron-filings pattern showing pole concentration, name the poles North and South, and explain with evidence why every fragment of a broken magnet retains both poles.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: A U-shaped magnet has iron filings spread on paper placed over it. Sketch or describe where the filings will cluster most densely, and explain what this tells you about where the poles of a U-shaped magnet are located.
expected_elements: Filings cluster most densely at the two open ends (tips) of the U-shaped magnet.
Filings are sparse along the curved middle section.
The poles are located at the two open tips of the U-shape.
The pattern shows that poles are always at the ends of the magnet, regardless of its shape.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who cannot sketch can describe the pattern in words; the key demonstration is the reasoning connecting dense filing zones to pole locations. Allow students who remember the bar-magnet sketch to use it as a reference for constructing the U-shape reasoning by analogy.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain — Earth's magnetism and directional alignment
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why a freely suspended magnet always aligns north–south by connecting it to Earth acting as a giant magnet, and can distinguish a magnet from an unmagnetised bar using the directional test.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: A bar magnet is suspended freely by a thread and allowed to come to rest. It is then disturbed and allowed to settle again. What consistent result will the student observe, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The magnet always settles along the north–south direction, because Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.

options.label: B
options.text: The magnet settles along the east–west direction, following the path of sunrise and sunset.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnet settles along the north–south direction, because gravity pulls it toward the nearest magnetic material in the ground.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnet settles in a different direction each time, because it is balanced perfectly.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing random direction shows the student did not connect the repeated-trial observation (always the same direction) to a causal explanation — they may not have attended to the consistency across trials in the activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing gravity and nearby magnetic material reflects a plausible but incorrect causal mechanism — the student understands that an external cause is needed but substitutes local gravity for Earth's global magnetism.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing east–west direction reveals confusion between the geographic east–west axis (associated with sun movement) and the magnetic north–south axis, a cross-concept confusion common at this stage.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who made and used the floating compass can connect this question directly to their observation that the needle pointed the same direction as the bar magnet — two forms of evidence for the same principle.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain — Earth's magnetism and directional alignment
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why a freely suspended magnet always aligns north–south by connecting it to Earth acting as a giant magnet, and can distinguish a magnet from an unmagnetised bar using the directional test.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: Priya has two identical-looking iron rods. She suspects one is a magnet and the other is plain iron. She suspends each rod freely by a thread. What result would confirm that Rod A is the magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: Rod A always comes to rest pointing in the same north–south direction, while Rod B rests in varying directions.

options.label: B
options.text: Rod A attracts Rod B when the two rods are brought close together.

options.label: C
options.text: Rod A is heavier than Rod B when weighed on a balance.

options.label: D
options.text: Rod A spins faster than Rod B when suspended and released.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing weight shows the student has not connected the directional property to magnet identification — they are using a non-relevant physical measurement to distinguish the rods.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing mutual attraction is a plausible but insufficient test: a magnet attracts plain iron as well, so attraction cannot distinguish a magnet from an unmagnetised bar — repulsion is the definitive test, and directional alignment is the test probed in this stage.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing spinning speed introduces a made-up criterion with no grounding in the chapter; the student may be guessing rather than reasoning from the directional property established in Stage 3.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who carried out the suspended-bar comparison in the activity can reason directly from memory; students who find it difficult to reason abstractly can be prompted: what did the bar do differently from the magnet when both were suspended and then disturbed?

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain — Earth's magnetism and directional alignment
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why a freely suspended magnet always aligns north–south by connecting it to Earth acting as a giant magnet, and can distinguish a magnet from an unmagnetised bar using the directional test.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: Explain how a magnetic compass works. In your answer, name the key part of the compass that makes it work, describe what it does, and state why it always points north.
expected_elements: The compass contains a freely rotating magnetised needle.
The needle aligns itself along the north–south direction when free to rotate.
This happens because Earth acts like a giant magnet, exerting a force on the compass needle.
The North-pointing end of the needle (typically painted red) indicates the direction of geographic north.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who built the floating compass can describe their own construction to ground the explanation; the homemade needle is functionally the same as the commercial compass needle. Students who process information visually may sketch the compass and annotate it rather than write full sentences.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state and apply the attraction–repulsion rule for pole pairs, use repulsion as the definitive test for identifying a magnet, and conclude from evidence that non-magnetic materials do not block magnetic effects.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: A bar magnet is placed on pencils so it can roll freely. Another magnet's South pole is brought close to the resting magnet's South pole. What will happen, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The resting magnet will roll away from the approaching pole, because like poles repel each other.

options.label: B
options.text: The resting magnet will roll toward the approaching pole, because opposite poles always attract.

options.label: C
options.text: The resting magnet will spin in place, because the poles cancel each other out.

options.label: D
options.text: The resting magnet will stay still, because South poles are neutral toward each other.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing attraction with the explanation 'opposite poles attract' reveals that the student has confused like and unlike poles — they either reversed the rule or did not attend to the fact that both poles in this scenario are South poles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing neutral response shows the student has not grasped that like poles actively repel; they may be conflating a null result with no interaction, missing that repulsion is a directed force.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing spinning reflects an invented response with no chapter grounding; the student cannot recall the rule and has defaulted to an arbitrary guess.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who remember the rolling magnet activity can replay the S–S trial mentally; students who learn better through language can be prompted to recite the rule (like repels, unlike attracts) before applying it.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate interactions — attraction and repulsion between poles
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state and apply the attraction–repulsion rule for pole pairs, use repulsion as the definitive test for identifying a magnet, and conclude from evidence that non-magnetic materials do not block magnetic effects.

competency.competency_text: Describe the properties of a magnet (natural and artificial; Earth as a magnet).

assessment_items.question_text: Rohan has two rods that look identical. He brings one end of Rod X close to the North pole of a known magnet and finds that it is attracted. He concludes that Rod X must be a magnet with its South pole facing the known magnet. His classmate says the conclusion is wrong. Who is correct, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Rohan is correct — a rod that is attracted to a magnet is always itself a magnet.

options.label: B
options.text: Rohan is correct — attraction to a North pole always means the attracted end is a South pole.

options.label: C
options.text: The classmate is correct — attraction alone cannot prove Rod X is a magnet, because plain iron is also attracted to both poles of a magnet.

options.label: D
options.text: The classmate is correct — attraction to a North pole means the attracted end must also be a North pole.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing Rohan's conclusion as correct shows the student knows the unlike-poles-attract rule but has not grasped its limitation — that plain iron (a magnetic material) is also attracted to a magnet, making attraction alone an insufficient test for magnet identity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing the classmate as correct but for the wrong reason (same poles attract) shows a double error — the student both agrees with the correct verdict and inverts the attraction rule simultaneously.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'attracted therefore a magnet' is the core misconception about the sufficiency of the attraction test — it would make every piece of iron a magnet, which contradicts the chapter's explicit treatment of iron as a magnetic but unmagnetised material.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who tested the iron bar in the rolling-magnet activity will recall that the iron bar was attracted to both poles of the magnet without being a magnet — that memory is the direct evidence needed to evaluate Rohan's claim.

assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student placed a bar magnet at a fixed distance from a compass and recorded the needle deflection with each material interposed between them. What conclusion does this data support? Explain your reasoning using the data.
expected_elements: The compass needle deflects by the same amount regardless of which non-magnetic material is placed between the magnet and compass.
This shows that non-magnetic materials do not block or reduce magnetic effects.
The magnetic force passes through non-magnetic materials such as cardboard, wood, plastic, and glass.
The student's data provides evidence for this conclusion because deflection is equal to the baseline in every trial.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to find out whether an unmarked rod is a magnet, a piece of iron, or a piece of plastic. She brings one end of the rod close to the North pole of a known magnet and observes attraction. What must she do next to tell a magnet from a piece of iron, and what result would confirm the rod is definitely a magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: Bring the same end of the rod close to the North pole again — if the rod is repelled, it is a magnet with a North pole at that end.

options.label: B
options.text: Bring the same end of the rod close to the South pole of the known magnet — if the rod is still attracted, it is iron, not a magnet.

options.label: C
options.text: Suspend the rod freely — if it aligns north–south, it is a magnet; if it rests randomly, it is iron.

options.label: D
options.text: Weigh the rod — a magnet will be heavier than a plain iron rod of the same size.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing weight reveals the student cannot identify the relevant property test — they have reverted to a physical measurement (mass) that has no connection to magnetic identity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing free suspension is a valid test for directional property but does not use repulsion — the student knows that magnets align north–south but has not identified repulsion as the more direct and definitive test for magnet identity in this scenario.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing attraction to the South pole as an iron indicator inverts the logic — both iron and a South-pole magnet would be attracted to a North pole, and both iron and a North-pole magnet would be attracted to a South pole; neither observation produces a distinguishing result, confirming that attraction alone cannot identify a magnet.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who designed test sequences in the closing investigation unit can draw directly on their written procedure; students who find multi-step reasoning difficult can be prompted to ask: which interaction — attraction or repulsion — is possible only if the rod is itself a magnet?

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can design and execute a multi-step investigation to determine whether an unknown object is a magnet, a magnetic material, or a non-magnetic material — including pole identification — by selecting and sequencing relevant property tests and defending each conclusion with evidence.

assessment_items.question_text: Magnets must be stored carefully. The chapter recommends storing pairs of bar magnets with unlike poles adjacent and a wooden piece between them, with soft-iron keeper bars placed across the ends. Which property of magnets makes it important to keep the poles adjacent rather than end-to-end with like poles facing?

options.label: A
options.text: Like poles facing each other would transfer magnetism from one magnet to the other, doubling the strength of one and halving the other.

options.label: B
options.text: Like poles repel each other, so keeping like poles facing would push the magnets apart and could reduce their magnetism over time.

options.label: C
options.text: Magnets stored with unlike poles adjacent will demagnetise each other because opposite poles cancel out.

options.label: D
options.text: Unlike poles attract so strongly that magnets stored with unlike poles adjacent will fuse together permanently.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing permanent fusion reveals a misapplication of the unlike-poles-attract rule — the student knows attraction occurs but exaggerates it to an irreversible physical joining, confusing magnetic force with chemical bonding.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing demagnetisation by opposite poles reflects a misconception that unlike poles cancel each other out — the student has borrowed a physical concept (cancellation) without grounding it in what the chapter says about storage.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing magnetism transfer introduces a completely invented mechanism; the student cannot identify the relevant chapter property and has constructed a plausible-sounding but unfounded explanation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who analysed the storage rules in the application units can reason from their written explanations; students who struggle with evaluation-level questions can be supported by first asking them to state the like-poles rule and then apply it to the storage scenario.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'I can always tell whether an object is a magnet by checking whether it attracts iron.' Evaluate this claim. Is attraction to iron a sufficient test? Explain what additional test is needed and why, using specific properties of magnets from this chapter.
look_for: Correctly identifies that attraction to iron is not sufficient because plain iron (a magnetic material) also attracts to a magnet, so the iron would be attracted to both a magnet and another piece of iron in some configurations.
Identifies repulsion as the additional and definitive test: only a magnet can repel — a plain iron bar is never repelled by either pole of a magnet.
Connects the repulsion test to the like-poles rule from the interaction investigation.
Uses precise chapter vocabulary: magnetic material, magnet, poles, repulsion, attraction.
Provides a clear logical structure: what the attraction test can determine, what it cannot determine, and why repulsion resolves the ambiguity.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who designed the identification procedure in the closing unit have already worked through this logic in practice — they can draw on their written test sequence. Students who find extended writing challenging can be offered a sentence-frame structure: 'Attraction is not enough because ___ . The additional test is ___ . This works because ___.'

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Four unmarked objects (P, Q, R, S) were each tested using the four-step procedure shown. Use the results in each row to determine whether each object is a magnet, a magnetic material (such as iron), or a non-magnetic material. assessment_items.scaffold: For each object, ask: Does it respond to a magnet at all? (Steps 1 and 2 together tell you.) If it responds, does it ever get repelled? (Steps 2 and 4 tell you.) OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to select and sequence property tests and defend conclusions with evidence — a data table recording multi-step test results is the most direct vehicle for that demonstration, requiring interpretation of patterns across rows and columns rather than recall.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can integrate multiple magnet properties — attraction, repulsion, directional alignment — into a coherent identification procedure, correctly reading which combination of results is decisive and explaining the logic of repulsion as the magnet-specific test.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the four steps into three diagnostic questions, guiding students who feel overwhelmed by the full table to process one property at a time before synthesising; a teacher can observe which students need the scaffold and which proceed directly to the conclusion column.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses correctly classify all four objects, identify repulsion (Step 4 for Q; the S–N response for S) as the decisive evidence, and explain the logic precisely (repulsion is possible only between two like poles, so only a magnet can repel). Weak responses classify P and R correctly (straightforward cases) but misclassify Q or S, and name only attraction as their evidence without addressing why repulsion is the decisive differentiator. Object S (attracted by N, repelled by S — indicating S-pole end facing the test) is the hardest case and is the best discriminator between strong and weak responses.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the full four-column table difficult can be directed to complete P and R first (clear non-magnet cases) before tackling Q and S; students who work better verbally can talk through each row with a partner before writing. The scaffold questions can serve as sentence starters for students who struggle with extended written explanation.
